20	\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
24	every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
25	categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
26	concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
27	tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
28	profiling.
29	
30	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
31	fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
32	cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
33	code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
34	traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
35	nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
36	the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.
37	
38	\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
39	break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
40	pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
41	using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
42	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
43	fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
44	query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
45	not separate profiler objects.
46	
47	We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
48	Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
49	semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
50	buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
51	oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
52	positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
53	cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
54	median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
55	improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth action labels, leave-dataset-out
56	mapping achieves V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets, and
57	learned boundary derivation beats simple baselines on 4/5 families
58	(RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
59	budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
60	surface.
61	\end{abstract}

65	%% ===================================================================
66	\section{Introduction}
67	
68	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
69	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
70	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
71	thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
72	to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
73	tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
74	distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
75	tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
76	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
77	events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
78	single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
79	that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
80	distribution grouped by semantic work category.
81	
82	This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
83	profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
84	instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
85	tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
86	millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
87	represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
88	enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
89	path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
90	assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
91	variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
92	error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
93	is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
94	unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
95	calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
96	across agent families and trace formats.
97	
98	This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
99	flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
100	\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
101	actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
102	local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
103	events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
104	that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
105	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
106	activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
107	chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
108	operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
109	projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
110	data.
111	
112	This paper makes three contributions:
113	
114	\begin{enumerate}
115	\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
116	  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
117	  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
118	  profiling. The key obstacle is that fixed session/span hierarchies
119	  cannot fold by semantic category, and natural-language prompts lack
120	  the deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
121	  (\S\ref{sec:background}).
122	\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
123	  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
124	  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
125	  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
126	  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
127	  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
128	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
129	  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
130	  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
131	  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
132	  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels
133	  consistent with ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
134	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
135	\end{enumerate}

138	\section{Background and Motivation}
139	\label{sec:background}
140	
141	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
142	
143	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
144	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
145	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
146	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
147	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
148	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
149	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
150	
151	These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
152	skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
153	nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
154	This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
155	span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
156	the execution context.
157	
158	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
159	
160	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
161	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
162	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
163	ways.
164	
165	\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
166	A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
167	may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
168	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
169	performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
170	merged without external logic.
171	
172	\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
173	Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
174	\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
175	\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
176	LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.
177	
178	\paragraph{Concrete example.}
179	In a real development project, the system effect
180	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
181	across 325 sessions. A flat process summary or a span-grouped view shows
182	a single ``cargo test'' counter. But this counter aggregates tests
183	triggered by 48 distinct prompt intents: \texttt{refactor} accounts for
184	only 32\% of the weight; the remaining 68\% comes from \texttt{review},
185	\texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and others. No
186	existing trace tool disaggregates this automatically.
187	
188	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
189	
190	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
191	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
192	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
193	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
194	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
195	\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
196	frames.
197	
198	Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language:
199	``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
200	share no characters. Tool calls, GUI actions, and process events are
201	named heterogeneously across agent families. If raw event names are
202	used as flame-graph frames, every prompt produces a unique bar and
203	folding collapses.
204	
205	These observations yield three design requirements:
206	
207	\begin{description}
208	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
209	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
210	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
211	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
212	  objects.
213	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
214	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
215	  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
216	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
217	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
218	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
219	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
220	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
221	\end{description}
222	
223	%% ===================================================================
224	\section{Design}
225	\label{sec:design}
226	
227	The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
228	
229	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
230	
231	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
232	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
233	abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
234	additive measures.
235	
236	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
237	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
238	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
239	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
240	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
241	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
242	This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
243	at the object-model level.
244	
245	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
246	
247	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
248	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
249	representation:
250	
251	\begin{small}
252	\begin{verbatim}
253	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
254	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
255	\end{verbatim}
256	\end{small}
257	
258	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
259	execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
260	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
261	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
262	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
263	
264	This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
265	\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
266	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
267	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
268	it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
269	provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.
270	
271	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
272	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
273	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
274	nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four questions:
275	
276	\begin{table}[t]
277	\centering\small
278	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
279	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
280	\label{tab:views}
281	\begin{tabular}{llll}
282	\toprule
283	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
284	\midrule
285	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
286	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
287	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
288	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
289	\bottomrule
290	\end{tabular}
291	\end{table}

294	\centering
295	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-architecture.pdf}
296	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
297	[Architecture: Agent trace files (Codex/Claude JSONL, benchmark JSONL)
298	$\to$ Parser / Importer $\to$ Intent Recognition (regex / LLM / clustering)
299	or Mapping Rules $\to$ Operations with fields $\to$ Stack query
300	$(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ $\to$ Folded stacks $\to$ Flame graph / pprof /
301	JSON]}}
302	\caption{System architecture. Local agent histories enter through
303	\texttt{agent-session} parsing; public datasets enter as operation JSONL.
304	Both paths produce operations; the stack query and output are identical.}
305	\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
306	recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
307	\label{fig:architecture}
308	\end{figure}
309	
310	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
311	
312	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
313	folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
314	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
315	this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
316	short, stable labels before stack construction.
317	
318	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
319	
320	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
321	The production default. Rules have the form
322	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
323	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
324	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
325	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
326	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
327	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
328	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
329	version-controllable.
330	
331	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
332	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
333	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
334	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
335	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
336	
337	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
338	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
339	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
340	
341	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
342	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
343	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
344	
345	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
346	
347	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
348	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
349	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
350	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
351	before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
352	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
353	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
354	
355	This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
356	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
357	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
358	stack query works identically on both.
359	
360	%% ===================================================================
361	\section{Implementation}
362	\label{sec:impl}
363	
364	\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
365	
366	\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
367	The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
368	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
369	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
370	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
371	semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
372	semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
373	instrumentation.
374	
375	\paragraph{Dataset import.}
376	Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
377	(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
378	Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
379	non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.
380	
381	\paragraph{Output formats.}
382	\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
383	\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
384	text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
385	SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
386	the same input and profile spec.
387	
388	\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
389	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
390	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
391	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
392	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
393	tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
394	run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
395	runs'' (profiling).

398	\section{Evaluation}
399	\label{sec:eval}
400	
401	We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
402	case studies and a reproducibility check.
403	
404	\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
405	We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
406	local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
407	multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
408	observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
409	mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
410	(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
411	mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
412	collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
413	oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
414	OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
415	requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
416	fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
417	changing only the stack fields.

442	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
443	
444	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
445	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
446	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
447	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
448	multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.
449	
450	\begin{table}[t]
451	\centering\small
452	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
453	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
454	\label{tab:mixing}
455	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
456	\toprule
457	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
458	\midrule
459	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
460	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
461	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
462	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
463	\bottomrule
464	\end{tabular}
465	\end{table}
466	
467	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
468	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
469	into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
470	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
471	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
472	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
473	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
474	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
475	
476	A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
477	appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
478	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
479	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
480	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
481	
482	A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
483	the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
484	information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$).
485	
486	The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
487	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
488	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
489	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
490	tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
491	questions over the same operations.
492	
493	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
494	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
495

497	ground-truth-labeled problems in real agent traces. The evaluation

711	\section{Related Work}
712	
713	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
714	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
715	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
716	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
717	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
718	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
719	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
720	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
721	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
722	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
723	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
724	agent-trajectory labels.
725	
726	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
727	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
728	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
729	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
730	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
731	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
732	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
733	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
734	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
735	cross-session aggregate profiling.
736	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
737	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
738	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
739	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
740	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
741	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
742	aggregation where width represents cost.
743	
744	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
745	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
746	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
747	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
748	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
749	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
750	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
751	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
752	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
753	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

756	\section{Discussion}
757	
758	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
759	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
760	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
761	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
762	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
763	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
764	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
765	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
766	understand why.
767	
768	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
769	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
770	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
771	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
772	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
773	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
774	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
775	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
776	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
777	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
778	for human inspection.
779	
780	\paragraph{Limitations.}
781	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
782	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
783	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
784	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
785	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
786	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
787	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
788	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
789	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
790	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
791	engineering work, not design obstacles.

794	\section{Conclusion}
795	
796	\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
797	semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
798	depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
799	local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
800	that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
801	traces.
802	
803	Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat
804	summaries merge (RQ1). Operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
805	problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat summaries and 45\% less
806	fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown, with actionable
807	configuration diagnosis (RQ2). Intent recognition produces labels that agree with ground-truth
808	annotations on 7/9 public datasets (V-measure ${>}0.7$), with learned
809	boundary derivation beating simple baselines on 4/5 families (RQ3). Case

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
profiling.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
not separate profiler objects.

We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth action labels, leave-dataset-out
mapping achieves V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets, and
learned boundary derivation beats simple baselines on 4/5 families
(RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
surface.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that fixed session/span hierarchies
  cannot fold by semantic category, and natural-language prompts lack
  the deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:background}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels
  consistent with ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary or a span-grouped view shows
a single ``cargo test'' counter. But this counter aggregates tests
triggered by 48 distinct prompt intents: \texttt{refactor} accounts for
only 32\% of the weight; the remaining 68\% comes from \texttt{review},
\texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and others. No
existing trace tool disaggregates this automatically.

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language:
``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
share no characters. Tool calls, GUI actions, and process events are
named heterogeneously across agent families. If raw event names are
used as flame-graph frames, every prompt produces a unique bar and
folding collapses.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
at the object-model level.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four questions:

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude

\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}

\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
questions over the same operations.

misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

\section{Conclusion}

\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
traces.

Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat

Now let me assess the scope findings.

---

## Phase 0 — Scope Review

### 1. Fundamental contribution identity

The paper presents three interwoven ideas but never names one as primary:

- **(a) The two-abstraction model** (operation + operation stack) — most space in Design
- **(b) Intent recognition** — described as "the hard problem" in §3.3 and given its own RQ
- **(c) The hidden-label evaluation methodology** — the most technically novel part of the evaluation

The introduction's contribution list frames (a) and (b) under "Design" and (c) under "Evaluation," treating them as equal. But a reviewer will ask: **which one is the paper about?** The insight that "agent observability needs profiling, not just debugging" is the actual thesis—(a), (b), and (c) are supporting evidence. That thesis is implied but never stated as a single sentence.

### 2. Scope assessment

The scope sits in a reasonable middle ground. It does not overclaim "we solve agent observability" (good). It does risk reading as "we built a tool" if the insight is not foregrounded (see finding M1).

### 3. RQ overlap and coverage

- **RQ1 (separation)** and **RQ3 (label quality)** partly overlap: the permutation test in RQ1 (lines 482–484) already tests whether labels are meaningful, and the V-measure table in RQ3 tests whether mapping-derived labels match ground truth. Both address "are the labels good enough?" from different angles, but neither section acknowledges the other.
- **RQ2 (localization)** is clean and self-contained.
- The "actionability" sub-section inside RQ2 (lines 551–569) could be its own paragraph or RQ. It answers a different question ("which knobs matter?") than the localization question ("can groups find positives?"), but cramming both under RQ2 is acceptable for space.

### 4. Claim–evidence mismatch

The paper claims to provide **profiling**—aggregate views of where budget goes. But the primary quantitative evaluation (RQ2) measures **localization**—whether top-ranked groups contain hidden positives. These are different things:
- Profiling answers: "40% of tokens go to review"
- Localization answers: "the top-5 groups contain 18.8% of the failures"

RQ1's mixing metric is closer to profiling, but it measures separation, not actionable insight. The case studies (§5.6) do show profiling insights, but they are qualitative, not quantified.

### 5. Strongest counter-argument

"Operations are JSON records with fields; operation stacks are GROUP BY on those fields. This is a data-engineering pattern, not a research contribution. The intent-recognition step is regex + a small LLM, both off-the-shelf. The hidden-label benchmark is the interesting part, but it evaluates a ranking problem, not profiling."

---

## Findings

### Must-fix

**M1 — §1 Introduction: Missing explicit thesis statement** (lines 98–110)
The paper describes the system but never states the thesis as a crisp sentence. The reader must infer it from context.
**Fix:** Add one sentence after line 97: *"The central insight is that agent observability requires profiling—aggregate, semantic, cross-session cost attribution—not only per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers."* Then frame (a), (b), (c) as consequences.

**M2 — §5.1/§5.3 RQ1–RQ3 overlap on label quality** (lines 482–484 vs. 572–650)
RQ1's permutation test already argues labels are meaningful. RQ3's ground-truth V-measure argues the same from a different angle. Neither cross-references the other.
**Fix:** In RQ1 (after the permutation paragraph), add a forward reference: "RQ3 evaluates the same question against ground-truth annotations." In RQ3's opening, add: "RQ1 established via permutation testing that labels carry non-random information; here we test alignment with ground-truth annotations." This makes the relationship explicit and avoids a reviewer thinking the two are redundant.

**M3 — §5 Evaluation: Profiling claim vs. localization evidence** (lines 494–569)
The paper's framing is "agent observability needs profiling." RQ2 evaluates localization/ranking, not profiling per se. A reviewer will note the gap.
**Fix:** Either (a) reframe the RQ2 introduction to explain why localization is the right proxy for profiling quality ("A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems; we evaluate this correspondence"), or (b) add a quantitative profiling-specific metric to RQ1 (e.g., what fraction of total budget the top-3 semantic categories explain, versus the top-3 session-based categories). Option (a) is simpler and only requires a sentence.

### Should-fix

**S1 — §1 Contribution 1 labeled "Problem" reads oddly** (line 115)
Identifying the aggregation gap is a framing contribution, not a problem-statement contribution. Labeling it "Problem" suggests the paper's main contribution is noticing a gap, which undersells the work.
**Fix:** Relabel as "Observation" or fold into the Design contribution: "We observe a structural gap ... and design a profiler that addresses it."

**S2 — §3 Design section opening is terse** (line 227)
"The three requirements from §2 drive the design." is too brief for a section opener. It should preview what the reader is about to learn.
**Fix:** Expand to 2–3 sentences: "The three requirements from §2 drive the design. We introduce two abstractions—operations (§3.1) and operation stacks (§3.2)—that satisfy R1 and R2, and a pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (§3.3) that satisfies R3."

**S3 — Abstract beat 4 (results) is too long** (lines 47–60)
The abstract devotes 14 lines to results—more than beats 1–3 combined. The RQ-by-RQ enumeration reads like an evaluation-section preview, not a summary.
**Fix:** Compress to 3–4 lines: keep one headline number per RQ, drop the AP/patch details.

### Consider

**C1 — §2.3 R1/R2/R3 descriptions are slightly generic.**
R1 ("uniform record type") and R2 ("query-time aggregation") sound like general database design. Tying them to the profiling domain more tightly—e.g., R2 could reference "folded-stack depth" rather than "aggregation shapes"—would sharpen the framing.

**C2 — §6 Related Work: Datadog/Laminar paragraph has no citations.**
The Datadog and Laminar claims (lines 736–742) are uncited. Add product-documentation URLs or remove the comparison.

**C3 — Case studies subsection is not linked to any RQ.**
The case studies float between RQ3 and Reproducibility. If they are evidence for "profiling produces useful aggregate views," link them explicitly to the profiling claim (M3's fix would help).
